title: How the Draft Conversion Practices Bill affects health professionals and young people
label: 12 November 2026 · Oral evidence, third session
summary: Witnesses from the Memorandum of Understanding coalition, the British Association of Gender Identity Specialists, the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy (BACP), and a clinical psychologist who worked at the Tavistock discussed how services for gender and sexual-identity matters operate, what the Bill would change, and what needs clarifying. They supported a law banning abusive conversion practices but urged clearer drafting, stronger reference to professional regulation, careful definition of “harm” (to avoid criminalising normal therapeutic distress), and special protections and competent assessment for children and neurodivergent young people.

glossary.definition: Memorandum of Understanding: a coalition of professional bodies setting out shared standards opposing conversion practices.
Attempts to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity, especially coercive or harmful methods.
An approach that affirms a person's gender identity and may include social changes and medical treatments such as hormones or surgery.
When a person who previously changed their gender presentation or had treatment later stops or reverses those changes.
The former NHS Gender Identity Development Service for young people, closed after review of its practices.
A professional register approved by the Professional Standards Authority that sets standards for non-statutory regulated health professionals.
Statutory UK healthcare regulators: HCPC regulates certain psychologists and therapists; GMC regulates doctors.

chapters.title: What services exist and what the MOU stands for
chapters.takeaway: There is a mix of NHS, private and voluntary services; the Memorandum of Understanding unites bodies against conversion practices and supports a legal ban.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re looking at how services for gender identity and sexual orientation operate in England and Wales. Could you outline current provision?

turns.speaker: Dr Igi Moon
turns.text: Services include private, NHS and voluntary sectors. The MOU brings together organisations that work on sexual orientation and gender identity to set common ethical standards and oppose conversion practices.

turns.speaker: Dr Alison Berner
turns.text: For gender identity healthcare there are around ten adult NHS gender services across the UK, plus newer young-person services set up after the Tavistock closure. Medical steps like hormones and surgery follow assessment and referral.

turns.speaker: Lord Hope of Craighead
turns.text: Should healthcare exemptions in the Bill treat sexual orientation and transgender care differently?

turns.speaker: Dr Alison Berner
turns.text: No. In gender healthcare we make a diagnosis to allow medical treatment. Sexual orientation is discussed in healthcare but isn’t a diagnostic category the same way. The Bill should protect both without distinguishing them in healthcare.

turns.speaker: Lord Hope of Craighead
turns.text: Should age make a difference—children around puberty versus adults?

turns.speaker: Dr Alison Berner
turns.text: Clinically we assess and give space for reflection at any age. Our role is not to convert someone to a particular identity. That principle applies equally to young people and adults.

turns.speaker: Dr Igi Moon
turns.text: I agree. The MOU’s position is not age-specific; member organisations handle youth issues through their own rules and regulators. The MOU aims to insist no identity is preferable to another and that safe exploration is offered.

chapters.title: The healthcare exemption and the need for regulation
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses want the Bill’s healthcare exemption to protect regulated professionals only and to be backed by clear guidance so ordinary therapy isn't chilled.

turns.speaker: Naz Shah
turns.text: Could an overly wide law chill therapists and make fewer people want to work in this area?

turns.speaker: Dr Igi Moon
turns.text: The MOU supports a legal ban. Therapists are regulated and should not be frightened of honest exploration. Regulation and supervision are key; a well-drafted Bill and good guidance should avoid chilling lawful practice.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: Clause 1(9)(b) speaks of procedures 'similar to medical or surgical care but not provided in connection with a medical condition.' Could that let anyone claiming to provide therapy wrongly use the exemption?

turns.speaker: Dr Alison Berner
turns.text: The exemption should apply only to regulated professionals. Regulation allows enforcement and protects the public; without that caveat the exemption risks being misused.

turns.speaker: Dr Igi Moon
turns.text: I agree: requiring statutory regulation or PSA-accredited registration provides a safety net and ensures accountability for professionals.

turns.speaker: Lord Hope of Craighead
turns.text: Should regulation handle misconduct before we get to criminal prosecution?

turns.speaker: Dr Alison Berner
turns.text: Yes. Regulators should investigate first. The Bill envisages prosecution only where conduct is well below professional standards and causes severe harm—akin to gross negligence for a healthcare professional.

turns.speaker: Baroness Browning
turns.text: What about people who present as therapists but aren’t statutorily regulated—are they outside the Bill and free to continue harmful practices?

turns.speaker: Dr Alison Berner
turns.text: That’s the concern. Adding a requirement that those offering care are under a regulator or on a PSA-accredited register would close that loophole and protect the public.

chapters.title: Defining harm, intent and what the Bill should capture
chapters.takeaway: Practitioners want the law to distinguish normal therapeutic distress from harmful conduct; they ask for 'serious' or similar qualifiers and detailed implementation guidance.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is the Bill’s wording right to capture abusive practices without criminalising ordinary therapy?

turns.speaker: Dr Lisa Morrison
turns.text: Ethical, good therapy won’t be conversion practice. But therapy often causes distress as part of treatment. We recommend qualifying 'distress'—for example 'serious' or 'prolonged and serious'—so normal therapeutic distress isn’t misread as criminal harm.

turns.speaker: Dr Anna Hutchinson
turns.text: I agree. Courts deciding subjective 'alarm or distress' risks testing the law on frontline clinicians. If harm is only defined in court cases, practitioners could become fearful of working with young people.

turns.speaker: Lord Hope of Craighead
turns.text: The draft uses 'serious alarm or distress' that 'has a substantial adverse effect on day-to-day activities.' Is that safe, or still too broad?

turns.speaker: Dr Lisa Morrison
turns.text: If read as a whole it’s acceptable; the problem is the potential for partial readings. Repeating or qualifying 'serious' reduces misinterpretation and the risk of vexatious complaints.

turns.speaker: Olivia Bailey
turns.text: Wouldn’t a court be the right neutral arbiter if someone claims they were harmed?

turns.speaker: Dr Anna Hutchinson
turns.text: A court is neutral, but we shouldn't force every interpretative question into litigation. Practitioners could be dragged through costly investigations for subjective complaints. Clearer definitions and professional guidance would help avoid that.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: Intent and a course of behaviour aimed at changing identity are part of the offence. If a therapy is genuinely exploratory, surely it won’t meet that intent test even if it’s distressing?

turns.speaker: Dr Anna Hutchinson
turns.text: Intent is hard to evidence. Adolescents may later perceive that therapy changed them and infer intent. That subjectivity worries clinicians: how do you prove or disprove intent years later?

turns.speaker: Dr Lisa Morrison
turns.text: Implementation guidance and professional-body guidance on good practice, plus public awareness of what good therapy looks like, will be crucial to reduce ambiguity about intent, content, context and professional standards.

chapters.title: Children, neurodiversity and gender-affirming care
chapters.takeaway: Young people—especially neurodivergent or otherwise vulnerable youth—need specialist, evidence-informed assessment; the Bill must protect them from abuse while avoiding deterring clinicians from working with this group.

turns.speaker: Baroness Browning
turns.text: Autistic young people were overrepresented at the Tavistock. Should only practitioners experienced with neurodiversity work with such cases?

turns.speaker: Dr Anna Hutchinson
turns.text: Vulnerable youth, including many who are neurodivergent, need careful, developmentally informed assessment. The field is politically polarised and evidence about long-term outcomes of medical pathways is weak. Clinicians must be cautious and competent.

turns.speaker: Dr Lisa Morrison
turns.text: Competency is central: specialist training, up-to-date CPD, and honest recognition of limits. If a practitioner lacks the skills, they should refer. Regulation and PSA-accredited registers help ensure minimum competencies.

turns.speaker: Dr Anna Hutchinson
turns.text: My worry is this: some clinicians are already accused of being 'conversion therapists' simply for questioning or being cautious. The Bill may intensify that fear and make it harder to recruit experienced staff, which could harm young people.

turns.speaker: Naz Shah
turns.text: Parents don’t have the same exemption as clinicians—if a discussion at home alarms a child, parents could face legal risk. Is that justified?

turns.speaker: Dr Anna Hutchinson
turns.text: Parents often have distressing safety conversations. The Bill gives professionals protections that parents don’t have. That gap needs thought because parents play a safeguarding role and may need to discuss risks frankly.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: Which is the greater risk: passing the Bill and deterring clinicians, or not passing it and leaving abusive conversion practices unaddressed?

turns.speaker: Dr Anna Hutchinson
turns.text: We need both protections. Stop abusive practices, yes—but avoid making clinicians so afraid they won’t assess or support young people properly. Balance means clearer definitions, guidance and competence requirements.

turns.speaker: Dr Lisa Morrison
turns.text: Practically, the Committee should press for detailed implementation guidance, a role for professional bodies to define good practice, PSA-accredited registers for non-statutory professions, and a public-awareness campaign so people understand what ethical therapy looks like.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We must finish as one witness has a hard stop. If you have anything to add in writing, please do. We appreciate your time and evidence.
